---
title: "Perceptual (in)sensitivity"
---

Listeners whose native language lacks contrastive word-level prosody often show a selective insensitivity in processing lexical stress contrasts, a phenomenon known as stress "deafness." This insensitivity is most reliably observed in sequence recall tasks that combine memory load with phonetic variability, conditions under which purely acoustic encoding strategies become unavailable and successful performance requires abstract phonological encoding. It remains unclear, however, whether the deficit observed for lexical stress extends to other word-level prosodic categories, in particular lexical pitch accent. In my research, I explore this question by comparing native French listeners, speakers of a language with no lexical prosodic contrasts, with native Serbian listeners on a sequence recall task involving the four lexical pitch-accent categories of Standard Serbian (long-falling, long-rising, short-falling, short-rising), alongside a segmental control contrast. I hypothesize that if stress deafness reflects the absence of prosodic marking in the lexicon, French listeners should show the insensitivity to pitch-accent sequences relative to the segmental baseline, and this insensitivity should exceed that of Serbian listeners. If, instead, listeners can recruit more general prosodic or psychoacoustic resources to encode unfamiliar pitch-based categories, French listeners should show no disproportionate pitch-accent impairment. I found that French listeners do not differ from Serbian listeners on the recall of pitch-accent sequences. Serbian listeners benefit from vowel length, whereas French listeners are better on pitch-only contrasts. The results argue against a strong form of the lexical-marking account of stress deafness. Our results argue for a nuanced account in which lexical prosodic marking, target-system structure, and cue-weighting strategies jointly determine adult listeners’ success in encoding unfamiliar word-level prosody. 

However, the task we use is a Sequence Recall Task (SRT) which in its design comprises an increased cognitive load and phonetic variability so as to induce the "deafness" effect. In a less controlled and less loaded design, the listeners could perform differently. Therefore, we carried out a study with an opposite type of task - free classification task. The study has been published in Canadian Journal of Linguistics. The details of the study can be checked here.
